paragraphs.text: SAYINGS AND INTERPRETATIONS OF PARABLES OF THE HOLY GOSPEL. Question 1. “Go into the village opposite, and you will find a man carrying a jar of water.” What is the city? The Church. What is the jar of water? Holy baptism. Who is the man? The Forerunner. What is the upper room? The kingdom of heaven. Question 2. “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.” Who is the king? God. Who is the debtor of the ten thousand talents? The man who, though steeped in many sins, has enjoyed God’s long-suffering. Who is the one [owing] the hundred denarii (80)? The one who was under the man who owed ten thousand talents. That man had himself received long-suffering, yet [?] he showed himself cruel and harsh toward his fellow servant. Another parable, 3. “A certain man had two sons, and he said to the one, ‘Go into the vineyard.’ And he said, ‘I will not go,’ and he went. And he came also to the other, and the other said, ‘I go,’ and did not

Who is the man? God. Who is the one who said “I go,” and did not go? The Jews. Who is the one who said “I will not go,” and went? The people from the Gentiles. Another parable, 4. “The land of a certain rich man brought forth plentifully.” Who is the man? Judas, and [?] those like him who are greedy and love money. Another, 5. “Go into the village opposite, and you will find a donkey tied, and a colt.” What is the village? The world. The donkey is the Jews; the colt, those [?] Christ. For the colt is the irrationality of the Gentiles, and

Another, 6. “Go into the city to a certain man, and say to him, ‘The Teacher says: I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.’” What is the city? Hades. Who is the certain man? Adam; for he was going to raise him from the dead. Another question, 7. “Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees.” Answer. The root is faith; the tree, the man; the axe, the man’s end. Another, 8. “A certain man built his house upon the rock.” Who is the man? Saint Peter; the rock, Christ; the house, faith; the wind— (80) “Who is the one … the hundred denarii”: supply “owing.” [?] “the hundred denarii”: supply “owing.” Ed. Patrol.

the devil. The one who built on the sand is Judas; for the sand is unfruitfulness. Another, 9. “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who gave a wedding feast for his son.” Who is the king? God. Who is the son? Christ. Who are the invited? The prophets and apostles. Who are those who refused? The Jews. Who are those who came? Those from the Gentiles. Who is the one without a wedding garment? Judas, and those like him who rush unworthily upon the [?]. Another, 10. “The Lord said to Peter: Go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a stater. Give it for me and for yourself.” What is the sea? The world. What is the hook? The word of God. The fish is Christ. The stater is the cross of the Lord, on which both he and Peter were to be crucified. Another, 11. “A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me…’” Who is the man? God. The two sons? The righteous and the sinners. The younger son is the one whose mind is unstable. The share that falls to him is the oracles of God and his commandments. Another, 12. “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive a kingdom.” The man is God; the far country, his coming upon earth; the kingdom, the second coming; the servants, the prophets, the apostles, and the martyrs. The mina is the grace that Judas received, and so also is the talent. Another, 13. “A certain man planted a vineyard and set a hedge around it.” The man is God; the vineyard, the world; the winepress, baptism; the tower, faith; the tenants, the Jews; the servants, prophets, apostles, and martyrs. He sent them to preach, and they killed them, and likewise the only-begotten Son and Word of God as well; and the kingdom was taken from them and given to the Romans, who produce its fruits. But those wretches perished wretchedly because of their unbelief and hardness of heart. Another, 14. “The sower went out to sow his seed.” The seed is the word of God. The one that fell among the thorns is Judas, for he went away and hanged himself, and the birds of the air devoured him. That which fell on the good ground is the prophets and apostles. Another, 15. “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers.” The man is Adam; Jerusalem, paradise; Jericho, the world; the robbers, evil thoughts and the transgression; the priest, the prophets; the Levite, the Mosaic law; the Samaritan, Christ; the oil and wine, the precious body and blood, and holy baptism; the inn, the Church; the innkeeper, Saint Paul; the two denarii, the Old and the New Testament.

Another, 16. “A certain man went out early in the morning to hire laborers.” The man is God; the vineyard, the world; the laborers, the apostles. The one who came about the eleventh hour is Matthias, who was numbered with the eleven apostles. Another, 17. “A certain woman had a drachma and lost it.” Who is the woman? The Church. What is the drachma?

Another, 18. “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field.” Who is the treasure? Christ. Who are those who bought it? Joseph and Nicodemus, or rather the holy Theotokos. 19. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour.” What is the leaven? Faith. And the three measures of flour? The Savior’s resurrection on the third day. Question 20. Why does the Baptist call the Jews a brood of vipers? Answer. Because this creature eats through its mother’s belly and so comes out. That is just what these people did: they became parricides and consumed their teachers and prophets out of envy. For they stoned Moses, and they sawed Isaiah in two with a wooden saw. Question 21. Why, when John had been handed over, did Jesus withdraw to Galilee? Answer. To teach us to flee temptations, but to stand firm nobly when we have fallen into them. Question 22. What sin did the fig tree commit, that Christ withered it? For what reason did he do it? And what

Answer. Since the Lord was about to undergo the passion, he did not want the disciples to think that he suffered because he was powerless and weak. So he shows his power on a lifeless thing, to show that he could have withered all who opposed him. But since he did not come to judge the world but to save it, as he himself said, he displays his power on the lifeless fig tree, while toward human beings he holds his love in reserve with boundless forbearance. Sin, too, is called a fig tree, which Christ our God cursed and withered. And there is also this: because it took the

[?] of the Samaritans [?] died, after them she lived in fornication; for no one was willing to approach her as a lawful wife. And since she could not bear to bridle her desire, she secretly kept the man who committed fornication with her, and he was neither openly known nor lawful. She had him as a husband in secret. Question 24. Who are the true worshipers, who worship neither on that mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth worship the

Answer. These are the people who dwell in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. Without any church assembly, enlightened by the divine Spirit through good works, they worship in spirit and truth God our Father who is in heaven. They live blamelessly and serve God with a pious mind, shining with all piety and dignity of virtue. They have no need of a church or a place; rather, making themselves temples by their good works, they please the Divine in every place and everywhere, serving him unceasingly and sincerely all the days of their

Question 25. What does this mean: “If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them”? Answer. That is, in any matter on which the soul agrees with the body, in a pious and virtuous request, God comes to be in their midst, as he conversed with Elijah on the mountain and with Daniel in the den and fulfilled their requests. Question 26. What does this mean: “Be well disposed to your adversary while you are on the way with him”? Answer. The body is the soul’s adversary. For these are opposed to each other, as Paul says. For we pummel and enslave the body, being well disposed to it through fasting and vigils and other hardships, so that it may no longer rise up against the soul through dishonorable passions. By “the way” he means this vain and deceitful life; for once the soul is released from the body and departs from this life and from the way, it can no longer do good. The “penny” is said to be even the very residue of a thought. Conscience, too, is called an adversary; for it reproves us secretly in the heart and holds us back from evil, and if we do not listen to it, in the end it hands us over at the judgment seat of God, and we shall give account both for great sins and for trivial and very small ones. Question 27. What does this mean: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed”? Answer. He says this on account of his humanity, because “Though he was rich, he humbled himself to the point of death, even death on

a cross.” And it is great and luxuriant in leaves on account of his divinity. The birds of the air in its branches are the prophets and apostles, and the evangelists themselves, perching there. Question 28. What does this mean: “You shall not make a sisoe from the hair of your head”? Answer. Some have interpreted the sisoe differently; but I think the law is forbidding that cutting of the hair. For the Greeks were accustomed not to cut the hair on the crown of their children’s heads, but to leave the locks, and after a time to dedicate them to the demons. Question 29. Why did Christ breathe on his disciples, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit”? Answer. Just as in the case of the blind man he made clay and anointed his eyes, to show that he is the one who in the beginning fashioned man from clay, in the same way he breathed on the disciples, showing that he is the one who gave breath and life to human beings through the ancient breathing into Adam. And by saying to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he gave them, through the breathing, authority and grace to forgive sins. Through the descent at holy Pentecost he granted the working of baptism and of signs. That is why he says, “But you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit, and you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” For before the passion the apostles performed their healings not in the Holy Spirit, but by the authority and command given them by Christ. “For the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” He was glorified when he was raised from the dead. In speaking of the “Holy Spirit” he does not mean the hypostasis of the Holy Spirit, for that always was and is and will be, but the gift of the Holy Spirit, which came down upon Christ’s disciples on the tenth day after the ascension, the fiftieth after the resurrection. Question 30. Who is the unjust judge, who neither fears God nor regards man? Answer. God; for he has no God whom he would fear, nor any man whom he would regard. “There was a widow in that city.” Who is that widow? The soul of every human being, which once had the devil as husband, [?]

“yet I will vindicate her, so that she may not wear me out by her coming.” And the Lord adds, saying, “Hear what the unjust judge says”—that is, God, since he judges and condemns the unjust. “For the law is not laid down for the righteous.” Question 33. How are we to understand, “Let him who has a cloak sell it and buy a sword”? Answer. The Lord said this because he wished to make known to the apostles his betrayal and the assault of the Jews. So he neither kept entirely silent, lest they be thrown into confusion by a sudden assault, nor again revealed it entirely, lest they be gripped by some cowardice. Question 34. How will one who loves his soul lose it? Answer. The one who loves his soul is the one who carries out its improper desires; the one who hates it is the one who does not yield to it when it commands harmful things; and the one who wishes to lose it is the one who, contrary to what is right, longs to escape the dangers and afflictions and temptations that come upon it. So, just as he called the loss suffered for his sake in dangers “salvation,” so he will find it unto eternal life. Question 35. What does this mean: “If your right eye or your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw

Answer. The Lord did not say this about the members of the body—far from it!—but about friends and relatives; for we are members of one another. So, he says, if you have a friend or relative who is as necessary to you as a right eye or hand—as Job said, “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame”—and you see that your soul is being harmed by him, cut him off from you. For there is no fellowship between light and darkness, especially if they share in some hypocrisy and deceit. Of Chrysostom, 36. “A certain man had a fig tree in his vineyard.” Answer. Scripture is accustomed to call the soul that is in sins a fig tree; the vineyard is the Church of the faithful; the vinedressers are the angels. Since, then, those who live in the Church unworthily (81) of the faith are called not a vineyard but a fig tree—having been planted in it, as is likely, from youth through baptism, but altering their way of life [?] up to old age—the long-suffering God fittingly says to the vinedresser, that is, to the angel of the Church: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on the fig tree and have found none. Cut it down; why should it even use up the ground?” And he says: “Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure.” The three years among human beings, then, in which God comes seeking fruit, are the three stages of human (81) “they live unworthy [lives]” [?].

life, that is, as children, young men, and elders. For many, having repented in old age itself, been dug around through afflictions, and received manure through temptations, have borne the fruit of virtue. Of Cyril, 37. Why is the Church called “Church,” and why “catholic”? Answer. “Church” (ekklēsia), because all are called out (ekkaleisthai); “catholic,” because it is spread throughout (kath’ holou) the world. Question 38. Where does the word “heresy” (hairesis) come from? Answer. From choosing (haireisthai) something of one’s own, and this from [?]

Text 39. “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath.” Interpretation. Note that God did not make winter. For it is written, “Summer and spring, you fashioned them.” By “flight” he means the time when the soul is separated from the body. He calls sins “winter,” and negligence “Sabbath”; and woe to the soul that is in sin and despondency and negligence. Another text, 40. “The stone which the builders rejected.” Interpretation. The stone is Christ, who was rejected by the scribes and Pharisees and the elders of the people of the Jews, and became the head of the Church of the Gentiles. [?] He is called this because he holds the nations together in faith in one concord. For since the descendants of the Greeks and of the Jews have believed in Christ, Christ was for this reason likened to a corner, because he joined their offspring together in the faith. Christ is also called the cornerstone in another sense. When a house is built, the builders place at the corner of the wall a cornerstone, that is, one with an angle at its edge. Set at the edge of the wall, such a stone joins and holds the two walls together at once. In this way, then, Christ too is called the cornerstone, because he joined the two peoples together at once, the people of the Jews and the people from the Gentiles; and for this reason he has been named the cornerstone. Question. What is it that Christ said to Peter…? [?] the crowds, having Christ in their midst, some of them came secretly behind him and struck him, while others asked him, to test him: “Tell us, who from among the people struck you secretly? If you know, prophesy and tell us; show us from the crowd the one who struck you, and we will know that you are a prophet.” 41. What does this mean: “And bowing his head he gave up the spirit”? For all who die first expire, and then they bow their heads.

Answer. The Lord had accomplished all that was written—the incarnation, the birth, the baptism, the display of signs, the effective working of his teaching, the winning of the disciples, everything human, the passion, the crucifixion, the mockeries, the wounds of the nails. After he had fulfilled these, all that he had to suffer, only death remained. And death, being afraid, did not dare to approach him; for this reason Christ bowed his head, summoning it. For until he bowed his head, it did not dare to approach him. That is why the evangelist says, “And bowing his head he gave up the spirit.” Question 42. Why did Christ cry out on the cross with a loud voice? Answer. To show his power, and to terrify the Jews and bring them to faith. For that voice split the rocks, tore the veil of the temple, shook the earth, and opened the tombs. And not even so did the senseless Jews understand. Question 43. How did Mary see the Lord, and in what manner? For she was standing at the tomb weeping before the angels, her bearing gloomy and her face downcast. How, then, did she see him walking and coming behind her? Answer. It was like this. The angels were sitting in front of her and saw Christ coming behind her; she could not see behind her. But the angels, sitting opposite her, saw Christ coming behind her and immediately stood up. When the woman saw the angels spring up, she was astonished, and she turned around to see what the angels had seen, and she saw Jesus coming. This is the reason Mary saw the Lord when she turned around. Question 44. Why did Christ ask his disciples for something to eat after the resurrection, and nothing else was found except a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb? Answer. Some have interpreted the honeycomb as salt; such words are the mythmaking of babblers. For the honeycomb and the piece of broiled fish are just what Scripture says they are. But the passage has a marvelous interpretation, very deep and of the most exact anagogical sense. The meaning of this reading is as follows. The fish is likened to the harsh way of life of the ascetics, who have subdued the flesh by fasts and vigils and other hardships, crucified themselves to the world and to pleasures, renounced moisture and the foods of this life, subdued themselves by dryness, and walk the ascetic way, as Christ commanded: “Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it”—that is, in fasts and vigils and other hardships. Now hear how the fish is likened to asceticism, or hardship. A human being is like the fish. (83) Matt. 13 [?].

For just as a fish, while it is in the sea, holds all its moisture and lives with its blood and all its slime, but when it is caught and taken out of the water it dies, and when it is put on the fire it is roasted and dried and loses all its impurity, so it is with a human being. While he is in the midst of life, he lives in the grip of passion for pleasures and unbridled desires. But when he withdraws from the world and lives in ascetic discipline and hardship in the desert, warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, then he is dried out of his passions and cleansed of all impurity, and through the virtues he becomes a sacrifice well-pleasing to God. Just as the fish becomes fit for food once it has been roasted on coals, so too a human being, cleansed by the heat of the Holy Spirit, becomes an acceptable sacrifice to the Lord. The honeycomb from the beehive also has an interpretation of the same kind. We should ask, then, why the honey was not without the comb. There is comb without honey, and there is honey without comb, but in that place both were found together. Listen to how this is. The honey stands for the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, which he was going to pour out on the apostles and on all the faithful. The comb stands for the seal that he gives to all the faithful through baptism. For a treasure is safer the more securely it is sealed up with wax. In the same way, the wealth of divine grace remains inviolable in a person who has the seal of holy baptism, the sign of the cross, and faith in

Question 45. Know that our Lord and God Jesus Christ was made flesh of the Holy Spirit and of Mary, ever-virgin, and became man, taking on everything human except sin and weakness. He worked miracles, was crucified, and rose on the third day according to the Scriptures. After all this he was taken up and sat down at the right hand of God. When you hear of God's right hand, do not picture places or shapes of glory, for right and left belong to things that have bounds. God is unformed, unlimited, without shape and without bounds. So when you hear of the right hand of God, understand it as the glory and honour of God. The Son of God, who is also God, was taken up afterward, as has been said, once he had fulfilled the whole plan of salvation. But the Holy Spirit, who came down on the holy disciples at holy Pentecost and was poured out on all flesh, was not taken up. He passes from generation to generation into everyone. According to how he finds each person, he dwells on that person in proportion to his purity, and he tastes sweeter than honey in the soul. Question 46. What did Christ mean when he said, 'Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not

be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come'? Interpretation. Christ said this because he is twofold in essence, God and man. Anyone who rejects him by blaspheming against his flesh will be forgiven if he repents, but the one who blasphemes against [?] ... showing the third face, which is like a man's, as most clearly describing his coming as a man. The fourth, which is like a flying eagle, makes plain the gift of the Spirit flying down upon the Church. The Gospels agree with these, and Christ is enthroned among them. The Gospel according to John tells of his sovereign and glorious begetting from his Father, saying: 'In the beginning was the Word.' That is why he is also given the name of the eagle. He strode through empty air to the heights [?] ..., was initiated there into the ineffable mysteries, drew up the hidden things of theology [?] ..., and wrote of the unspeakable and incomprehensible begetting of the Son of God. The Gospel according to Luke begins with Zechariah the priest. The one according to Matthew records his human birth: 'The book of the genealogy.' And the one according to Mark begins: 'The beginning of the gospel.' For this reason four universal covenants were given to humankind. The first came at Noah's flood, with the sign of the bow. The second was with Abraham, with the sign of circumcision. The third came through Moses in the giving of the Law. The fourth came through the holy Gospel, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[?] Various interpretations [?]. Question 47. What does 'The earth was invisible and unformed' mean? Answer. It means that the earth had not yet been adorned. Because the water lay over it, it was invisible, that is, unseen and hidden. It was unformed, that is, unadorned and incomplete, for it did not yet have flowers or meadows or plants or any growth. Question 48. What spirit was moving over the

Answer. Some think it is the all-holy Spirit giving life to the nature of the waters. I say, however, that the words 'was moving over' fittingly indicate the moving substance of the air, just as David says about the God of all: 'He will blow with his wind, and the waters will flow.' Question 49. Why did he speak of one gathering of the wat-

-ers and then afterward name many? For he says, 'The water under heaven was gathered into its gatherings.' Answer. The waters have one nature and form one gathering. He named the gatherings in the plural because the Indian Sea is one, the Pontic another and the Atlantic another, the Propontis is one, the Aegean another, and the Ionian Gulf yet another. Beyond these lies the greatest sea, which some call Ocean. So he called it one gathering because it is gathered together, and gatherings because it is divided. Question 50. What light separated the day and the night before the sun existed? For the sun and the other lights came into being later. 'And there was evening, and there was morning, a day.' How should this be understood, when there was not yet a sun? Answer. God spoke the light, and it came to be. That light was what separated the day and the night. God said, 'Let there be light,' and there was light. This is not the sun. Listen to what this light is. It is the morning light, which rises and lights up the world from early morning before the sun comes up. Let no one think that the brightness which dawns quickly and lights up the world before the sun belongs to the sun. Rather, it is what Scripture speaks of: 'And God said, Let there be light, and there was light.' This light was abundant and exceedingly bright, and God then divided it into the lights: the sun, the moon and the rest. Question 51. What does 'Let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years' mean? Answer. By 'signs' he means knowing the time for sowing, for harvest and for the grape-gathering, the season in which to plant and when to cut timber. For each season has its own proper work. The year has four seasons, and each season has its own work. Question 52. Why did God make the plants before the lights, but the animals after them? Answer. The plants have no soul and no eyes, and they were created before the lights because they could bear the brilliance of the light. The animals came into being later, after the lights, because God divided the first great light he had made among the lights. It was dispersed and became gentler. If this had not happened, the animals could not have endured the great blaze and the brilliance of all that fire. That is why the animals came into being later, so that they could bear the brilliance of the fire. Question 53. Why did God, after fashioning man from the earth, not fashion Eve from it as well, but fashion her from his side? Answer. So that people would have no reason to say that the [?] dust

from which he fashioned Adam was different [?], and that the good and virtuous people come from that, while the bad, the wicked and the crooked come from Eve. That is why God fashioned them from one dust. Question 54. Man is a better and more wonderful work of God than the rest, for God made him king over the earth and made him according to his image and likeness. How is it, then, that God fashioned him last of all? Answer. Think of a king who is about to go to some city. First people make everything ready for him, arranging his gifts and all his service and comfort, and only after this does the king arrive. So it was with man. God first took care of everything for his rest. He prepared his dwelling and everything he would need for his comfort, and after that he fashioned him. Question 55. What does 'Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness' mean? What is 'according to the image,' and what is 'according to likeness'? Answer. God does not have a human form as human beings do. Far from it! 'According to the image' means this: God reigns over the whole world and rules and holds authority over everything in heaven and on earth. In the same way man has been made ruler and king over all earthly things, and he freely does whatever he wishes, just as God does. This is 'according to the image.' 'According to likeness' means goodness and virtue. God is good and merciful, compassionate and just, patient and gentle, loving and sympathetic, peaceable and forbearing. He shows mercy to all people, feeds them, and displays his goodness toward all. In the same way he made and fashioned man, and he wants him to be adorned with every virtue and ... [?] to imitate God in every good work and in dignity, as far as a human being can. Question 56. To whom did God say, 'Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness'? Answer. Some of the ill-named heretics have gone so far as to claim that he said this to the angels and to the wicked demons. The fools do not understand that he did not say 'according to our images' but 'according to our image.' God, the angels and the demons do not share the same substance or the same image. I say that he foresaw that the Only-begotten would take flesh and become man and would take this nature from a Virgin. He therefore thought of himself as one person of God and man, and foresaw that one act of worship would be offered to him by all creation (Gen. 1:26),

and so he addressed his words to the only-begotten Son himself. Question 57. Which comes first and is the beginning, the night or the day? Answer. From the first making of the world, that is, from the fashioning of Adam, until the coming of Christ, the day came first. The divine Scripture says this when it tells that God said, 'Let there be light, and there was light,' and that 'God called the light day, and the darkness he called night.' Scripture puts the light first, and this is why the day came first. We began from the light and were later brought down into darkness, for we strayed from the straight road and fell into idols and the darkness of deceit. But from the coming of Christ, night once again begins first and takes precedence over day. That is why we begin our celebration of the following day's feast from the evening before. Listen to how this came about. In the beginning we fell from light into darkness, so the light came first and the darkness afterward. But Christ our God, the Sun of righteousness, has risen on the world and led us back from the darkness of error to the light of the knowledge of God. Since then we too begin from darkness and end in light. In this sense the night takes precedence: it gives us a beginning and sends us on toward the light. For in Scripture this life is called darkness, as the divine Paul says: 'Let us lay aside the works of darkness and put on the armour of light,' that is, of the age to come. For the age to come is light, and the weapons of that light are the virtues. That is why Christ said, 'Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you.' He called the virtues light, because a person can have them as long as he lives; after death he cannot acquire them. This age is called darkness because of its dark and lawless deeds. As Christ also said: 'Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.' To follow Christ means to do what pleases him and to keep his commandments. Such a person will never walk in darkness, that is, in the empty ways of this life. He will dwell in and [?] receive the eternal light of life in the age to come, together with the boundless joy and gladness of that place. Question 58. Did Adam and Eve realize that they were naked only after eating, or did they have this awareness even before eating? Answer. Very small infants do not naturally blush when their clothes are taken off; they acquire a sense of shame gradually, as their bodies grow. So it was with Adam and Eve. When they were first fashioned they were like infants, guileless

and with no share in sin, and they felt no shame at being without clothing. But once they had experienced sin, they covered their private parts with leaves. Question 59. What does 'Behold, Adam has become like one of us' mean? Answer. God says this as a rebuke, reproaching Adam for his presumption: 'Did what you imagined actually happen? Did you become a god, as the evil one told you when he deceived you?' For Adam wanted to rise higher and fell lower instead. Question 60. What does 'Its return is to you, and you shall rule over it' mean? Answer. God said this to Cain about the gift that had been offered: 'Let the very gift you brought come back to you, and you shall have authority over it. Do with it as you please, for I did not accept it.' Question 61. Why was it the righteous Abel who died, when it was Adam who had sinned? Answer. Because God did not want death to have a strong foundation. If Adam had died first, death would have had a firm footing, having received the sinner as its first corpse. But since it first received someone who was unjustly killed, its foundation is shaky and rotten. Question 62. What does 'Whoever kills Cain will release seven vengeances' mean? Answer. Among the crimes Cain dared to commit, the first sin was envy because Abel was preferred. The second was the deceit with which he spoke to his brother, saying, 'Let us go out into the plain.' The third was murder, adding evil to evil. The fourth was that killing his brother made the crime all the worse. The fifth was that he brought grief on his parents. The sixth was that he defiled the earth with blood. The seventh was that he lied to God, for when he was asked, 'Where is Abel your brother?' he said, 'I do not know.' So seven vengeances would have been released when Cain was killed. These are the seven vengeances: first, he provoked God to anger; second, he grieved his father; third, he made his mother childless; fourth, he killed his brother; fifth, he shed blood; sixth, he committed murder; seventh, he was the first to open Hades. Question 63. What does 'My guilt is too great for me to be allowed to live and not die' mean? Answer. It means 'My condemnation has become greater.' God's curse left Cain in such a state that the trembling and shaking of his limbs kept him from even putting food in his mouth. Question 64. What does Lamech mean when he says, 'I have killed a man'

Answer. He is not speaking of two men, as some have supposed, nor of Cain, as others have told in their fables, but of one man, and a young one: 'a man to my wounding, and a youth to my bruising,' that is, a man who was young in age. Lamech escaped punishment by confessing his sin. By passing sentence on himself, he prevented the divine sentence.

Question 65. Whom did Moses call sons of God when he said, 'The sons of God saw the daughters of men and took wives for themselves'? Answer. Seth was born of Adam; he was the third son, after Abel. Enosh was born of Seth, and he hoped [?] to call on the Lord God. So the children born of his line were called sons of God, just as we are called Christians after the name of Christ our Master. The race of Seth had been kept separate and did not mix with Cain's descendants, because of the curse the God of all had laid on Cain. Later, however, they saw that the daughters of Cain's kindred were beautiful. Bewitched, they took them as their wives and corrupted their own lineage. Question 66. What does 'Abraham looked up and saw, and behold, a ram caught by its horns in a sabek plant' mean? Answer. The sabek plant is the precious cross. Among the Hebrews, sabek is thought to mean remission and forgiveness. The ram caught in the sabek plant was offered as a sacrifice in place of Isaac, and it prefigured Christ, who was offered for us as a spotless victim and underwent death on the cross for our sake. 'For by his bruise we were all healed,' says Isaiah, 'and he suffers pain for us, and was wounded for our sins.' So just as that ram was offered in place of Isaac, Christ too was offered for us all. Question 67. What does Isaac mean when he says, 'See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field that the Lord has blessed. May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and wine, and let nations serve you,' and the rest?

Answer. The field is the world, the dew of heaven is the divinity, and the fatness of the earth is the humanity. Dew comes down invisibly but becomes visible when it gathers below. In the same way God the Word, who is invisible, was seen on earth through the flesh and lived among human beings. The grain and the wine are figures of the divine mysteries. All the nations serve the

Question 68. What does it mean that Jacob took three rods, a green one of storax, one of walnut and one of plane, and peeled them thin? Answer. Symbolically, the three rods are the three powers of the soul: the rational, the desiring and the spirited. Or else they are the three kinds of contemplation: of bodies, of bodiless beings and of the Holy Trinity. Or, more generally, the walnut stands for the practical life and the storax for the contemplative life, while by the plane tree he hinted at this world and its contemplation. Question 69. Why did Jacob look up and see the camp of God encamped there, and say, 'This is God's camp'? Answer. The camp of the angels appeared to Jacob so that he would take courage and not fear his brother Esau, for Esau wanted to kill him. That is also why he wrestled with an angel, and the angel said to him, 'You have overcome me, and are you afraid of a man?' And he knew that he had God

Question 70. What does 'Judah is a lion's whelp; from a shoot, my son, you went up; you lay down and slept like a lion,' and the rest mean? Answer. This applies to Christ. A lion is fearsome even when it sleeps, and in the same way the Lord's death is fearsome both to death and to the devil. He called him a lion and a lion's whelp because he is a king and a king's son. The words 'Who will rouse him?' show his unspeakable power, for he raised himself, as he had foretold when he said, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' Question 71. What does 'Binding his colt to the vine, and his donkey's colt to the tendril' mean? Answer. By the vine he means Jerusalem, and by the colt the people from the nations, as being untamed. The Lord hinted at this when he sent the disciples to untie the donkey and the colt on which no one had ever sat. No patriarch, no lawgiver and no prophet gave thought to the salvation of the nations. But the apostles, at his command, untied human nature, which was bound by sins. Question 72. What does 'He will wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape,' and the rest mean? Answer. He is speaking of Christ's passion. He calls the body a robe and the blood wine, since the Master also called the mystical wine his blood. And 'His eyes are joyful with wine' points to the gladness that follows the passion.
Answer. The devil, when he said to Eve, "Why is it that God said not to eat from the tree?" Question 74. What will become of the elements, the sun, the moon and the stars at the second [?]

Answer. They will be given a dwelling place in one part, but they will not be completely destroyed. Question 75. Why did God curse Cain, saying, "Cursed are you from the earth," but in Adam's case laid the curse on the earth, saying, "Cursed is the earth in your works"? Answer. Because Cain denied God and hid his sin, he brought the greater condemnation on himself. But Adam confessed, and so warded off much of the punishment. Whoever confesses his own faults obtains forgiveness. Question 76. What is "Why did the nations rage, and the peoples plot vain things?" Answer. By "nations" he means those of the Romans, that is, the race of the Franks, who crucified Christ. By "people" he means the head of the Jews. "The kings of the earth stood by": Pilate and Herod; "and the rulers": Annas and Caiaphas. "A psalm for the winepresses." Question 77. What does he mean by winepresses? Answer. The churches, in which the wine is poured out, that is, the holy blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, and [?] also his holy body. And the words of the prophet Isaiah, "I have trodden the winepress alone," mean this. A winepress is a vessel in which the grapes are trodden down. In the same way Christ trod down his enemies, both spiritual and visible. Let us also say this: Christ is the cluster and the grape. He pressed himself out by a voluntary wound and death, made the divine new wine drip out, and dyed himself red with his own blood. He is "alone" because Christ alone died for us: "For neither an angel nor an envoy, but the Lord himself saved us." Peter denied him at the time of the Passion, and the rest of the apostles fled. Question 78. What is "You who thirst, go to

Answer. The water signifies holy baptism, or the fountain of tears, that is, repentance. And "Come, buy, and eat and drink without money" means the holy baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise "The Lord will inhabit the flood" also points to holy baptism, since it floods away all sins. Interpretation 79. What is "The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire"?

Answer. This signifies the coming punishment of fire, since at Christ's command it will be divided. Fire has two powers. He will give the illuminating power to the righteous and the burning power to sinners. Interpretation 80. "The river of God is filled

Answer. The showers are the apostles, for they were filled with every kind of gift and grace. Every pure and virtuous person is also like this. In Scripture water and dew sometimes signify the gift of God, and sometimes temptations and the turmoil of the soul. When it says, "Whoever believes in me, rivers will flow from his belly," and "Like the dew of Hermon that comes down on the mountains of Zion," it means the gifts of the Holy Spirit. By the mountains of Zion it means spiritual people who live according to God. But when it says, "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul," and "Our soul has passed through the overwhelming water," it means the temptations of the soul. Question 81. What is "Ascending on high, you led captivity captive"? Answer. It means that Christ ascended the cross, plundered Hades and took it captive. This is also the meaning of the saying "The Lord said: From Bashan I will return," that is, from the cross I will return to Hades. Bashan is interpreted as "shame." The Jews regarded the cross as a shame and called it an instrument of the curse. But Christ sanctified it, since on it he accomplished the salvation of humankind. Question 82. What does "The rich became poor and went hungry" mean? Answer. Here he calls the Jews rich. They became poor because they killed the bread of life, and famine came on them. Question 83. What does "In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the land, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity" mean? Answer. It means this. Morning is the beginning of the day, and in the same way the suggestion of the enemy is the beginning of every sin. So he says "In the mornings I killed," that is: I kept watch over the beginnings of my thoughts and drove off their assaults; "and all the sinners," that is, the demons that work sin in me; "so as to destroy from the city of the Lord all," that is, from the soul, for the soul is the city of the Lord. "For I pursued," he says, "and killed their heads,

that is, their beginnings, so that I might destroy them from the soul and they would not work any iniquity or sin." Question 84. What does "Young lions roaring to snatch prey and to seek their food from God; the sun rose, and they gathered together and will lie down in their dens" mean? Answer. By young lions he means the prophets. They roared as they cried out, spoke and prophesied the incarnation of the Son of God. "The sun rose": that is, Christ came, and they fell silent. The prophets prophesied until John. Scripture says the same thing elsewhere: "Dark water in clouds of the air; at the brightness before him the clouds passed away." By dark water it means divine Scripture, since Moses received the law from God in the thick darkness on Sinai. The prophets too saw and made known the coming of Christ only dimly, darkly and faintly. Scripture calls the prophets clouds because they preached and poured out like water the divine word and law on the earth, blowing like winds, and this is the dark water. "At the brightness before him," that is, at his coming in the flesh before them, the clouds, meaning the prophets, ceased and [?]. Question 85. What is "Mount Zion, where you have dwelt"? Answer. Divine Scripture interprets "mountain" in many ways. Mount Zion is the site of Jerusalem, where our Lord and God Jesus Christ dwelt when he became incarnate on earth. Scripture also properly calls the all-holy Mother of God a mountain, as when it says, "The mountain in which God was pleased to dwell; for the Lord will dwell there to the end," and elsewhere, "God will come from Teman, and the Holy One from a shady and thickly wooded mountain." The holy Mother of God is called a mountain for this reason. People walking on the plain and scorched by the heat come near a mountain and are cooled in the shade of its trees, or ease the burning heat with its water. In the same way the pure Virgin became a refreshment for humankind. With the cool dew of her childbearing she revived human souls that were burning with sin, and she sheltered them in the shadow of her Son's wings. The demons are also called a mountain because of their swollen pride: "He who touches the mountains, and they smoke." That is, when he comes near the demons, they dissolve like smoke and vanish. Virtue is called a mountain too, as Gregory among the saints says: "For on this mountain God appears to men, descending from his own lofty height and leading us up from our lowliness below." Question 86. Why is virtue called a mountain? Answer. Because just as a mountain is higher than the earth

but lower than heaven, so is the person who practices virtue. He is higher than the earth because he is above the cares of life and the material things of the world. But he is lower than heaven, since he is still in this life and has not yet died and been wholly freed from this world. In this way he stands between heaven and earth like a mountain, as has been said. So when Scripture says, "The high mountains are for the deer," it means the lofty virtues, and by deer it means the souls of the saints. The souls of the saints move about in the lofty practices of the virtues as deer do on a mountain. And the rock that is a refuge for the hares is Christ, who is the refuge of those who live in the desert. Question 87. What does Scripture say about the dwelling of the heron? Answer. Some say the heron is a bird. This bird nests in a deserted place at the top of a tree. The small sparrows come and nest beneath it all around in the tree. The heron's dwelling leads them and sits over them, and the heron guards them from destructive snakes that want to harm them. Question 88. What does the Prophet mean when he says, "For the end: do not destroy; of David"? Answer. By "the end" the Prophet means the end of his own life. He prays that the end of his life may not come in such a way that he falls into some harm. If a person's whole life has been spent badly but its end turns out well, that is grace and glory. But if the end is ruined, that is misery. This is why the Prophet prays that the end of his life may be good, and it was for this purpose that he composed the psalm. Question 89. What does "The holy ones will boast in glory and rejoice upon their beds" mean? Answer. By "holy ones" he means spiritual and holy people, who boast on their beds after death. The beds are the dwelling places of the saints, which they find after death, and they rejoice in the kingdom of heaven. Divine Scripture, teaching and making plain what perfection in God is, has called it sleep, bed, couch and death. It calls it sleep, as when David says, "In peace I will lie down together and sleep": that is, I will reach that same goal and give myself to living in God, as the holy Apostle said, "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." It calls it a bed, as when it says, "The holy ones will boast in glory and rejoice upon their beds." A person who has lain down on his bed rests and sleeps sweetly. In the same way, someone made perfect in God, who has attained to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, rests in God and regards perfection in God as a bed. By the feet

of the bed it means the virtues. It calls it a couch, as when Solomon says, "Sixty mighty men surround it." When the virtuous person reaches perfection, the mighty ones, that is, the angels, surround him and stand round about him, as the one who said, "I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken." Divine Scripture is accustomed to call even an angel Lord, as with Manoah: "We have seen God," when God had appeared in a vision. David also called it death, saying, "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones." You see how divine Scripture has presented it as sleep, bed, couch and death. It called it death because whoever has died has been justified from sin. A dead man cannot return to life and sin again, and in the same way someone who has been counted worthy of this cannot turn back. Instead he says with David, "The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear?" and with Paul, "For whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's," and again, "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith." Having been perfected in this, the saints despised the world and did not count the pleasure of this world as pleasure. The martyrs despised tortures. Text 90. "The high praises of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands." Interpretation. The high praises of God are the teachings of the law and the spiritual ordinances. The spiritual teachers have gifts of grace from the Holy Spirit in their throat, that is, in their mouth and tongue, and with them they teach the people. The two-edged swords are the two Testaments, the old law and the new. A soldier carrying a two-edged sword slaughters the enemy and saves the people. In the same way the spiritual teachers have two-edged swords, the teachings of the Old and New Testaments. With these they execute vengeance on the nations and cast them into punishment, calling down wrath on them from God through their supplication to God. They also reprove the ordinary faithful and teach them what is good. When the people do not listen to them, but oppose what is good and despise them, then the teachers call down punishment on them too through prayer, to correct them. Their aim is that once chastened, the people may learn not to disobey God or his servants, for whoever listens to spiritual men listens to God, as Christ said. The spiritual do not inflict chastisement to harm but to benefit, to correct people toward the good and for the glory of God. They do so as zealots and avengers of God and haters of evil.

FROM THE EPISTLES OF PAUL. Question 91. "Glory and honor and peace to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no partiality with God. All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law." Interpretation. He praises all who do good. By "Greek" he does not mean the idolater, but the God-fearing person who does not believe in Christ and does not keep the old law, but is without the law. Such a person still names and reveres God and practices virtue. Even if he stumbles, he will be punished more lightly than the Jew, because the Jew transgresses the law and faces the greater accusation. When you hear "All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law," understand the lighter punishment; and when you hear "All who have sinned under the law," understand the worse punishment and retribution. Text 92. "For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also be in the likeness of his resurrection." Answer. "We have been planted together" means we have become partakers. The Lord's body was buried in the earth and made salvation spring up for the world. In the same way our body, buried in baptism, made righteousness spring up for us. The likeness is this: Christ died and rose on the third day, and in the same way we die in baptism and rise again. Plunging the child into the font three times and raising it up again signifies the death and the three-day resurrection of Christ. Question 93. What is "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God..." and the rest?

Answer. The law, he says, was too weak to justify man, because man could not bear the tyranny and burning of the flesh. So God sent his only-begotten Son, so that through his flesh he might condemn sin. As for "in the likeness of sinful flesh," he did not say "in sinful flesh," but "in the likeness." Christ's human flesh was made like human flesh in all things, since he was perfect man. But his flesh did not become sinful as ours is: "He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth." Question 94. What does "Give place to wrath" mean? Answer. Forgive the one who has grieved you, distressed you or wronged you. Leave vengeance to God, and he will arrange what is needed. And "Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves" means this: when you do something as a matter of prudent management for the salvation

of your brother, and everyone finds fault, but your own conscience does not condemn you, you are blessed. Question 95. What does "Since Jews ask for a sign and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified" mean? Answer. He means: if we say to a Jew, "Believe," he says, "Raise the dead, heal the mad." If we speak to a Greek, he demands a polished speech from us. But we preach Christ crucified, who is both the power behind the signs and the ocean of wisdom. They, however, take offense and think the preaching foolish when they hear of a crucified God. That is no wonder. People with weak eyes cannot look clearly at the sun, and it is the same with them. "The foolishness of God is wiser than men" refers to the cross. The wise, the philosophers and the powerful busied themselves and toiled over vain things and achieved nothing good. But the cross, which they thought foolishness, saved the world. That is why it is wiser than all, because it accomplished great things.

Question 96. And what does "The weakness of God is stronger than men" mean? Answer. By "the weakness of God" he means the mind of the apostles. They were simple and unlettered men, yet in a short time they caught the whole world in their net, kings and rulers, wise men and potentates

Text 97. "But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom." Answer. You see how he himself now calls wisdom what he earlier called foolishness. Here "mystery" first of all means God's plan of salvation. Neither angel nor any other created power knew this mystery and plan, that God was going to become incarnate on earth. When it came to pass, then all came to know it, as the Apostle says: "So that it might now be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places." Elsewhere he also uses "mystery" for the extraordinary works of God: the birth, the manger, the baptism, the cross, the death, the resurrection and the ascension. In the same way Gregory the Theologian among the saints calls the feasts mysteries in his Oration on the Holy Lights: "Again my Jesus, and again a mystery." He says this about the feast of the Baptism, and likewise in the other cases. Question 98. What does "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire" mean? Answer. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer the loss of the kingdom of heaven, but he himself will be saved as through fire. How will he be saved? That is,

he remains whole and intact in the fire and will not see death. Only his work will be burned up and destroyed. He himself remains intact, being punished for ever and ever, and will not be dissolved. Question 99. What does "A little leaven leavens the whole lump" mean? Answer. He says this about wicked and crooked people. Old leaven is small, yet it makes a great deal of flour rise. In the same way the evildoer, nourishing wickedness in himself, passes it on to others too, becomes a stumbling block and does harm to many. So he also says, "Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be new," that is: drive the wicked and crooked person out from among you, or flee from him, since all wickedness defiles a person. That is also why David, fleeing from the wicked, said, "I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not go in with transgressors. I have hated the assembly of evildoers." Why did he do this? Because he also says elsewhere, "With the holy you will be holy, with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse." Whatever kind of person lives with you, that is the kind of person he will make you. Question 100. What does "Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will do away with both the one and the other" mean? Answer. By "belly" he means gluttony, not the stomach. Foods, he says, have an affinity with gluttony, and gluttony with them. The glutton cannot serve God; instead he serves his own belly, carousing and gorging himself. So the Apostle abolished it, saying, "God will do away with both the one and the other," that is, the foods and gluttony. He did not abolish the stomach; God forbid! Listen to what he says: "The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord." So he did not abolish the stomach but gluttony, and not moderate food but excess, since fornication is born from these. That is why he says that the body was not given to be ruled by gluttony and fall into fornication, but to serve the Lord. As he says again earlier, "All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial; all things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anything." What he means is this: all the foods that God created to nourish man are good, and it is right for me to eat of all of them and be nourished. But I will not become a slave of foods, and gluttony will not master me [?]. It does me no good and builds up nothing good in me. So we are content with necessities alone and spurn what is superfluous, since it is not useful but actually harmful to me and breeds improper desires in those who possess it. Question 101. What does "And all were baptized into Moses" mean?

Answer. The crossing of the Israelite people through the Red Sea was a sign of baptism. Just as they crossed over and escaped the plot of their enemies, and were fed with manna in the desert, so those who are baptized are set free from the earthly Pharaoh and the Egyptian demons, and are fed with the heavenly bread of the Holy Spirit. [?] Since our subject is baptism, let us speak about it more clearly. On holy baptism. The first baptism was that of the Flood, to cut off sin. The second was that of Moses, when he crossed the Red Sea. It was a type: as the sea was there, so the water is in baptism; and as the cloud was there, so the Holy Spirit is here. Hear what that cloud was. When the Hebrews came out of Egypt with Moses, he sent [a cloud?] like a pillar of fire, and it gave them light at night, so that they could travel by night too and the Egyptians would not overtake them. And behind them went a cloud that overshadowed them, so that the Egyptians could not see them. This is the second baptism. The third is that of the Law, which the Hebrews had. Anyone who was unclean bathed in water and washed his garments, and so entered the camp. The fourth baptism is John's. It was introductory, not yet wholly spiritual, but only for repentance. The fifth is the one through our Lord Jesus Christ, with which he himself was also baptized. This one is wholly spiritual, and we too are baptized with it. The sixth is the baptism of tears, which is truly painful, like that of the man who washes his bed every night, repenting and lamenting over the sins he has committed. The seventh baptism is through martyrdom and blood, with which Christ himself was also baptized. It is far more venerable than the others, because it is not stained by later defilement. The eighth and last does not save but burns, punishing sinners endlessly and eternally. Question 102. What does it mean, “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God”? Answer. Anyone who feeds his own flesh until it is glutted cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Question 103. What does it mean, “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema. Maranatha”? Answer. That is: Separate him from the Church and the faithful, and let the one who does not believe be cut off from the people. For the Lord has come; that is what “Maranatha” means. Question 104. “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” [?]. Answer. That is: If anyone has believed in Christ, he has entered a different way of life. He has been born from above through the Spirit, and he lives not the life of sin but the life of the Spirit.

Question 105. “Three times I was shipwrecked.” Answer. He is speaking in a mystical riddle. Humanity was shipwrecked three times: first through the transgression; second in Noah's flood; and third when, after receiving the Law, the people fell away into idolatry. This lasted until Christ, the pilot of souls, came, raised the sail of the cross, and built us a voyage to heaven, free from storms. Question 106. “A night and a day I have spent in the deep.” Answer. By “a night and a day” he means the time spent in the darkness of error before Christ's coming. By “day” he means the life lived in the light of baptism after Christ's coming. Another interpretation: Some say he means he was sailing in the middle of the open sea; others, that he was swimming and keeping afloat where neither land nor mountain could be seen. Text 107. “A thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet me.” Interpretation. “Satan” means the adversary. So by “a messenger of Satan” he means Alexander the coppersmith, and Hymenaeus and Philetus. They tempted him and opposed him, saying that the resurrection had already happened. They seized him, threw him into prisons, and did him much harm. Text 108. “My grace is sufficient for you.” Answer. That is: My grace is sufficient for you, since you raise the dead, heal the blind, and perform the other signs. And though you are driven out and persecuted, you overcome your persecutors. Question 109. What does it mean, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world”? Answer. It means leaving behind this life and its cares, becoming dead to the passions and desires, and fasting, keeping vigil, and enduring hardship in ascetic discipline. As he says elsewhere too: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.” Question 110. What does it mean, “The dividing wall of the partition”

Answer. That is, the enmity that we human beings had toward God because of our sins. So the Lord and God became flesh and died. He destroyed the sin that separated us from God, made peace in all things, and made us sons of God, tearing up on the cross the written bond that stood against us. Hear what that bond was. When Adam transgressed the commandment, took from the tree with his hand and ate, the sin was written by his hand, and the devil held on to that document. But when Christ came upon the tree, that is, upon the cross, and his hands were wounded by the nails, he nailed it to the cross and blotted it out. For the devil himself, who held the bond of Adam's

transgression, tore it up himself, because Christ bound him on the cross. Question 111. What does it mean, “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you”? Answer. By “the sleeper” he means the one who lies in sins. For whoever lives in sins is said to be dead. And just as a dead man cannot move, so the one deadened by sins cannot move toward the good

Answer. He means the Holy Spirit. Whoever has no share in the Spirit has no strength against the opposing powers. “For our wrestling is not against blood and flesh,” that is, our war is not against human beings, “but against the principalities.” By “principalities” he means the demons, since they rule in this world, but over the works of darkness. And he says “in the heavenly places” because the demons do not fight us over some small matter but over heavenly goods. Because we are striving for the kingdom of heaven, they fight us fiercely. That is why we must always keep watch and conquer them by the power and grace of Christ. By “the shield of faith” he means sincere and ardent faith. Question 113. What does it mean, “Having put off the old man and put on the new, which is being renewed”? Answer. By “the old man” he means the first man, the one born from the fall of Adam, or the wickedness that comes from him and every vice. By “the new man” he means the life lived according to Christ, that is, a virtuous and good life. Question 114. What does it mean, “So that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope”? Answer. It is those who have no hope of resurrection who have reason to grieve. But notice how he said of Christ that he died and rose, while of ordinary people he said “those who have fallen asleep,” to show that those who sleep will rise. Question 115. What does it mean, “He did not count equality with God a thing to be seized”? Answer. What he means is this. The Son of God, who is God, wished to come down to earth and become flesh, and he was not afraid to step down from his rank. He did not possess the Godhead by robbery, the way someone holds a stolen thing and is afraid of losing it. Christ was not like that, God forbid! Being perfect God, he willed to become man as well. Question 116. “For this we declare to you by the word

coming of the Lord, will by no means go ahead of those who have fallen asleep.” “The living” are those who are found alive then at the resurrection. On that day there will be people who are found alive and will not see death, yet they will not go ahead of those who have fallen asleep. The dead will rise first, and after that the living will be changed and caught up together to meet the Lord in the air. Hear how this catching up will happen. When the Lord gives the command, that is, the order, the angels cry out, “Rise, the Bridegroom has come!” Then he will come down from heaven. First the dead will be raised; after that the living will also be changed and become incorruptible. Then all the saints and the worthy will be caught up by the clouds and will receive our Lord as he comes from the heavens. As it says, “And we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” This is the glory and the crown of the righteous. But sinners wait for him to come down. It is like a king coming to a city. The leading and distinguished citizens go out to meet him, while the poor and humble wait until he arrives in the city. Understand it this way with Christ too. When he comes down from heaven, all the righteous and good will be caught up into heaven to meet our Lord Jesus as he descends, while the sinners stand on the earth and wait. Text 117. “No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life, so that he may please the one who enlisted him.”

Interpretation. If a man about to serve an earthly king as a soldier cannot please him unless he leaves behind all the cares of this life, how much more is this true of one about to serve the heavenly king? Text 118. “And an athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.” Interpretation. If someone serves as a soldier and goes into battle, he is still not crowned unless he engages the enemy, strikes with the sword, and kills him. That is what competing according to the rules means. Text 119. “The farmer who labors ought to have the first share of the fruit.” Interpretation. He said this about spiritual teachers. The teacher who labors and struggles for his own sake and for the benefit of his disciples should receive his rewards from God first, and then the disciples. For when a farmer brings in his harvest, he first stores some of his produce in his own house, and then he gives either alms or payment to his creditors.

Another interpretation of the same text. Put another way: everyone who wishes to labor in the work of God, and to teach and benefit others, must as a teacher first practice the virtues, receive the gifts from God, and acquire the fruits of the Holy Spirit and the treasures of the knowledge of God's good things. Then he will be able to share these gifts with others. If someone wants to anoint another person but has no oil in his own hands, how can he give others what he does not have himself? Understand the teacher in the same way, as

Question 120. “Consider what I say.” Answer. Since he wrote everything to him in parables, he says, “Pay attention.” And they did not submit to the authority of Moses. Moses gave the order, and they killed three thousand of the people. This is what Scripture means when it says, “whose bodies fell in the

Text 121. “And every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty.” Interpretation. All who transgressed and disobeyed under the old law justly received punishment. Adam was condemned for his disobedience. Cain became accursed for his sin. Those in Noah's time who did evil were drowned in the flood. Those in Sodom who lived shamefully were terribly overwhelmed. And the Jews, who often rose up against the prophets, received blows, scourges, and punishments from God. So what he is saying now is this. In the Old Testament, everyone who set aside the Lord's command and disobeyed what was spoken through angels and prophets justly received punishment and brought God's wrath on himself. How then shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation, which was spoken to us neither through angels nor through prophets, but through Christ and God himself? In the Old Testament Moses was the minister of the law, but Christ is the minister of the New. These things, then, are far better than the old legislation. There a servant ministered the law, but here it is the Master, Christ. We ought to carry out what has been commanded without hesitation, so that the account we give is not even worse than that of the ancients. Text 122. “For it was not to angels that he subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking.” Interpretation. By “world” he means the judgment of the second coming, when he will repay each person according to his works. And “of which we are speaking” means the world for which we strive and in which we are all eager to be saved. The Apostle is saying that on that day God did not give the angels authority to judge the world, but has given all judgment to his Son. And since the Son of God, who is God, has all authority to judge the world, what will those who disobeyed his commands suffer? For if those who disobeyed the old law, which was given through an-
gels, suffered so much, even though the angels are not judges of the world, what will those suffer who disobeyed the Master himself? Text 123. “What is man, that you are mindful
Interpretation. By “man” and “son of man” he means Christ, since he is in all things consubstantial with the Father, as perfect God and perfect man. Text 124. “You made him a little lower than

Interpretation. By being made “a little lower” he means that Christ spent three days and three nights in Hades. Text 125. “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, in death.” Interpretation. The cross is the glory and honor of Christ, because countless good things came about through the cross. Death has been trampled down, the curse banished, Hades plundered, sin abolished, and the transgression annulled. Human nature has been freed from slavery to the passions, the devil bound, salvation planted, the resurrection made known, wickedness driven out, life has sprung up, and idolatry has been undone. And what is more wonderful still, even the ancient prophets of old were baptized by the blood and water that flowed from Christ's side. Hear how. Since the human body is made up of four elements, after death it dissolves back into them. So it was with Christ. The blood and water that poured from his holy side dissolved into the same place where the prophets' bodies had dissolved, that is, into the elements, and finding them there, it baptized them. If someone says that it baptized the bodies of unbelievers too, we answer: no. When water flows along, it waters and refreshes all the green plants it finds, but it does nothing for the dry ones. Understand this case in the same way. Text 126. “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him,” since the preaching had not yet [?] been proclaimed to the world. Interpretation. It was fitting for him, clearly meaning God the Father, through whom all things came into being and hold together, to make the author of life, that is, Christ, who brings many sons to the glory and kingdom of heaven, perfect. By “sons” he means spiritual and holy people. It was fitting, he says, for God the Father himself to show the author of our salvation, that is, Christ, to be perfect and glorious through sufferings. Question 127. What does it mean, “And of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man”? Answer. By “tabernacle” he means heaven, which no human being built, as people build church buildings on earth. It is not made with hands, since it was fashioned by the word of God.

Text 128. “All the saints through faith conquered kingdoms.” Interpretation. Abraham, Moses, Joshua son of Nun. “They worked righteousness”: Abraham, Phinehas, and David. “They obtained promises”: Joshua son of Nun and Caleb. “They stopped the mouths of lions”: Daniel in the pit. “They quenched the power of fire”: the three youths in the furnace. “They escaped the edge of the sword”: Elijah and David. “They were made strong out of weakness”: like Hezekiah. “They became mighty in war”: like Samson, who with a single jawbone of a donkey overthrew a thousand Philistines. “Women received back their dead by resurrection”: the Shunammite woman and the widow of Zarephath. “Others were tortured”: he means James the brother of the Lord and the others who were beheaded, for beheading is what “torture” means here. “Others experienced mockings and scourgings”: Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Micah. “They were stoned”: Stephen and Naboth. “They were sawn in two”: Isaiah, whom the Jews sawed with a wooden saw. “They were tempted”: like Job. “They died by the sword”: James, Zechariah, and the rest. “And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised.” That is, all these saints, though they were commended for having pleased God, have not yet enjoyed the kingdom of heaven and the good things promised to the righteous. They are waiting for the second coming, so that all may be crowned together in a single moment. This is what the Apostle means when he says, “since God had foreseen something better for us, that they should not be made perfect apart from us.” Half of them do not receive the promised good things without all the rest. They have the hope and the pledge, and they are separated from the sinners, but they have not yet received the fullness. For this is better: that all should enter the kingdom at one time, and all the saints together receive equally the good things of

God. Text 129. “Since we have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us.” Interpretation. He called them a cloud of witnesses because they refresh us like dew when we are held fast in sins and scorched by them, and they shelter us in the shade of their intercessions. Text 130. “Laying aside every weight, and the sin that so easily besets us.” Interpretation. By “weight” he means multitude. What he is saying is this: Since we have so great a multitude of holy martyrs, like a cloud refreshing us with dew, let us trust in the intercession of their prayers and imitate their virtues too. Let us throw off the whole weight of our sins and leave behind the sin that so easily besets us, and run the contest of virtue with endurance and patience. He called sin

“easily besetting” because it has no firm footing but quickly shifts and is undone. Sin has no root, and no fruit either. It is quickly destroyed and undone, cut down by the sword of repentance. Repentance is an axe that cuts out every evil. But repentance is not bending the knees. It is turning away from evil, toiling, lamenting, and praying to God for the forgiveness of past sins. It is called “repentance” (metanoia) because it moves the mind (nous) away from evil toward good.

OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS ATHANASIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA: SOME FURTHER QUESTIONS. Question 1. What is God? Answer. God is an intellectual essence, unseen and inexpressible. God is immaterial spirit, a sleepless eye, and an unmoved mind. God is the creative essence behind all creatures, both invisible and visible. Question 2. And why is God called “God” (Theos)? Answer. He is called Theos from theorein, “to behold,” because he beholds all things, as a beholder (theoros); so Theos means the one who sees all things. He is also called Theos from theein, “to run,” because he runs through all things spiritually and timelessly. For God is always present everywhere. Question 3. And how many gods are there? Answer. There is one God of gods and Lord of lords, and besides him there is no other. But human beings too are called gods by grace, as in the verse: “I said, You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High.”

Question 4. And since he is one, how do we call him [?] one God in three hypostases, Father, Son and Holy Spirit? For look, we are saying three, not one. Teach us, then, how God is one, and how again we speak of three persons in God. It seems wonderful to us that God is one and yet his persons are three.

Answer. Listen with understanding, and you will grasp the mystery of the Holy Trinity as far as the human mind is able to grasp it. As it seems to me, though, this can only be said as far as our words allow. For God cannot be put into words, and that is why we cannot comprehend his nature. Nor is he like us, a single person. If he were a single person, we would know him as we know one another. But God is one, and his persons are three. Now look at what follows. Just as the sun is one, and the sun has a ray and light, and there are three persons in the sun: the disc, the ray and the light. The disc is the [?] of the sun; the ray comes down shining like a torch and strikes the earth; and the light is what gives light, even in shaded [?] places where there is no ray. See, then: three persons, the disc, the ray and the light. Yet we do not speak of three suns but of one sun; nor do we speak of one person, but of three persons. If you are asked how many suns there are in the sky, you will say that there is one sun; but if you are asked how many persons the sun has, you will say three: the disc, the ray and the light. Understand God in the same way. God is one, but the persons of the one God are three: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. And from this learn that just as the sun has three persons, so the one God has three hypostases. For the sun's disc is a figure of the Father, the ray is a figure of the Son, and the light of the sun is a figure of the Holy Spirit. And say this: In the sun there are the disc, the ray and the light, yet we do not speak of three suns but of one and only one; likewise in God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one God, not three.
