And say this too: In the sun the disc, the ray and the light are inseparable, for they are not separated from one another; and for this reason God too is called one and not three, because the three persons of the one God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, are not separated from one another. And just as the sun's disc begets the ray and sends forth the light, so God the Father begets the Son and sends forth the Holy Spirit. Consider this with understanding. Just as the ray of the sun comes down from the sky to the earth, and is neither separated from the sun's disc, nor absent from the sky, nor from the earth, but is in the sun's disc, and in the sky, and on the earth, and everywhere, and is absent neither from the things above nor from the things below, so too the Son and Word of God came down to the earth, and was absent neither from the Father, nor from the heavens, nor from the earth; but he was inseparably in the bosom of the Father, and above and below and everywhere, and was absent from nothing. And just as the sun's light is both in the sun's disc

and in the ray, and in the sky, and on the earth, and enters into houses and goes everywhere, and gives light, so too the Holy Spirit is with the Father, and with the Son, and above and below, and enlightens every human being, and is never absent. For “the Holy Spirit,” says the apostle Paul, “searches all things, even the depths of God.” Consider, then: just as with someone we have never known, nor are able to know what he was like, when we see his portrait we grasp a little of the features of his face, so too, I ask you, think about God. For “no one has ever seen God.” How then can anyone comprehend him? But since God is light and is called light, we make an image of him from this light that we perceive with the senses, so that, as we said before, we depict the Holy Trinity in the figure of the sun, saying that the Father is the disc, the Son the ray, and the Holy Spirit light from light. And just as the disc, the ray and the light are one and three, divided without division, so God the Trinity, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, is one and three, divided in the persons, as with the sun, yet remaining undivided in nature. And just as the sun's disc alone is cause and unbegotten, while the ray is caused and begotten from the disc, and the light proceeds from the disc alone, sent through the ray and shining on the things around the earth, so too God the Father alone is cause of the other two and is unbegotten; the Son is caused and begotten from the Father alone; and the Spirit itself is caused and proceeds from the Father alone, but is sent into the world through the Son. Hold this, understand it, and believe it about God. But if the example of the sun is not enough for you to come to know the Godhead in three hypostases, look at another image of God: the human soul. For when God was about to fashion man, he said, “Let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness.” See then, man is the image of God, that is, the human soul. Now the human soul is one, yet it has three hypostases; the soul has three persons. How? Listen. The soul is one person; the soul begets the word, and see, the word is another person. The soul also sends forth the breath, and see, the breath is another person. Here are three persons: soul, word and breath. For the word and the breath belong to the soul, not to the body, since when the soul has left the body, neither word nor breath remains in the body, but the body lies there without breath and without speech. The word and the breath are with the soul; and from this it is clear that both the word and the breath come from the soul and are persons of the soul. And see then, the soul is one person, the word another person, and the breath yet another person. Here are three persons of the soul, but one soul, not three. For if you are asked how many souls a human being has, you will say one. But if you are asked how many

persons the soul has, it is right for you to say three, since soul, word and breath are one soul and three persons. The soul is a figure of the Father; the word of the soul is a figure of the Son and Word of God; and the breath of the soul is a figure of the Holy Spirit. For just as the soul is unbegotten, so God the Father is unbegotten; and just as the word is begotten from the soul, so the Word of God is begotten from the Father; and just as the breath proceeds from the soul, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. And say this: Soul, word and breath are one soul, not three, for the word and the breath are inseparable from the soul. Likewise Father, Son (that is, Word) and Spirit are one God, not three, for the Word and the divine Spirit are inseparable from the Father. And just as the soul is invisible, so God too is invisible. And so, when you ponder in your mind and ask how God is one, a unity, and yet in three hypostases, think of your own soul and say: Just as my soul is one, yet also has three hypostases, soul, word and breath, so God too is one, yet also has three hypostases, Father, Word and Holy Spirit. And say in your mind: If the soul, which is God's handiwork, and likewise the sun, has three hypostases while their nature is one, how much more God, the maker of these things! Is it not possible for him to be such that he is one in nature and three in hypostases? Indeed it truly is possible. For just as soul, word and breath are three persons and one nature of soul, not three souls, so Father, Word and Holy Spirit are three persons and one God in nature, not three gods. If you always reason in this way, you will never blaspheme against the Holy Trinity. But listen, beloved, to yet another image of God. Look: fire is one, and yet it has three hypostases. For the underlying fire itself is one; its power to burn is another person; and its power to give light is another person. See then, three persons of the one fire, namely the underlying fire, the burning and the giving of light; yet the nature of fire is one, not three. So it is with God: the Father is the fire, the Son the burning, and the Holy Spirit the giving of light. And just as with fire we call the fire, the burning and the giving of light, together with the underlying fire itself, one and not three, so with God too we speak of the three persons, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as one God, not three. And let this suffice concerning the knowledge of the Holy Trinity for the [?]

But listen to another mystery besides these. The human word has a twofold birth and is born on two occasions: once it is born from the soul, and again from the lips. A person's word is born from the soul when someone thinks of saying something. For the thought is called the first birth of the word, since he thinks of saying that word; but he does not speak it with his lips,

but the soul keeps the word in its bosom; and that thought is the first birth of the word from the soul. Yet even though the word is born from the soul in a first birth when the soul thinks of it, the soul does not reveal it but still keeps it. When it wishes to reveal the word, then it begets it from the lips. And this second birth of the word, from the lips, reveals the word to all, and the word is no longer called hidden but manifest. When the word is born through the lips, then everyone hears it and it becomes plain to all; and this birth through the lips is called the second birth of the word. So our word has two births: one from the soul, when it thinks of uttering the word, which is called the first birth; and another from the lips, which reveals the word to all people, which is called the second birth. Learn, then, exactly this: just as the human word has two births, one from the soul and another from the lips, so the Word of God has two births, one from God the Father, which is called the first birth, and another from the flesh, which is called the second birth. And just as our word, even when it has been born in its first birth from the soul, is nevertheless hidden and not revealed, but after its birth remains again in the bosom of the soul, so the Word of God, though he was begotten before the ages from God the Father, was not revealed to human beings but remained again in the Father's bosom. And just as our word, when we wish, is born from our lips and becomes plain to all who are near us, so the Word of God, when it pleased him, was born from the lips of the prophets and from the all-pure Mary, and then became plain to the whole world. For just as our word is revealed when it is born from our lips, so the Word of God, born from the flesh of Mary, ever-virgin, was revealed to the whole creation, and those who have believed in him are saved. And just as our word, when it is born from our lips, is absent neither from the soul, nor from our own lips, nor from the ears of those who hear, but is in the soul, and on our lips, and in the ears of the hearers, and is absent from nowhere, and even if a thousand thousands hear the word, the word is not diminished but always remains entirely full for us, so too the Word of God, though he was born from the Virgin Mary and from the lips of the prophets, was nevertheless absent neither from the Father, nor from the flesh, nor from all people, nor from the whole creation, but was present everywhere, and was not diminished but was entirely full. Understand this, then, about God the Word: he has a twofold birth, one from God the Father and one from the flesh; the one from the Father is before the ages, the one from the flesh is in the last days, just as our word is first born from the soul and then from the lips. And this is what concerns the two births of the Word

Question 5. What is common to the Holy Trinity?

Answer. The essence is common; being without beginning is common; power, goodness, wisdom and justice are common. For the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit have all things equally, except their own distinctive properties. For the distinctive property of the Father is being unbegotten, that of the Son being begotten, and that of the Holy Spirit proceeding.

Question 6. How many essences do you confess in God?

Answer. I say one essence, one nature, one form, one kind, one glory, one dignity and lordship.

Question 7. And how many hypostases do you confess in [?]

Answer. I confess three hypostases, three persons, three distinctive properties, three individuals and three characters.

Question 8. Why is the Father called Father?

Answer. God is called Father (Patēr) as the one who keeps (tērōn) all things (panta), as if he were the keeper of all.

Question 9. And why is the Son called Son?

Answer. He is called Son (huios) from the word hoios, meaning “of such a kind” and “like”; for such as the Father is, such is the Son; and by changing the o into u, we get huios. For the Son is like the

Question 10. And why is the Spirit called Spirit?

Answer. He is called Spirit (Pneuma) from perceiving every nod (pan neuma) swiftly, that is, every inclination is quickly perceived through him. “For the Holy Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.”

Question 11. How many causes are there in God?

Answer. I say there is one cause in God, and this is the Father. For the Father himself begets the Son and also sends forth the Spirit. Know, then, that the Father alone is cause; the Son is not cause, but caused. So the Father alone is cause, and the things caused are two, the Son and the Spirit. The Father is called cause because he begets and is not begotten, he sends forth and does not proceed. He begets the Son, and he also sends forth the Holy Spirit. And that is why the Father is called cause.

Question 12. And how many are caused?

Answer. Two are caused, the Son and the Spirit. The Son does not beget but is begotten, and that is why he is called caused. So if someone asks you, “How many causes do you confess in God?” say, “I say one cause.” “And which is this?” “The Father.” “And why is the Father called cause?” “Because he begets the Son and also sends forth the Spirit.” And if he asks you, “How many caused do you speak of in God?” say, “Two.” “Which are these?” “The Son and the Spirit.” “And why are they called caused?” “Because

Spirit, and does not send forth.”

Question 13. In the Holy Trinity, who is first [?]

Answer. In the Holy Trinity no one is first and no one is later; rather the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are together at once. That is why they are called co-eternal without beginning, and without beginning. What is called “without beginning” is that which exists before the beginning. So the Father is without beginning, the Son is without beginning, the Holy Spirit is without beginning. And it is not that one is first and another later; the three are together at once, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. That is why they both are, and are named, co-eternal without beginning.

Question 14. Explain this to us too: how is the Son and Word of God begotten from the Father? For this astonishes us.

Answer. Since God cannot be seen and cannot be put into words, we cannot explain this either. For how can anyone explain what he himself has never seen, nor ever heard from others? Yet from his works, I say, let us speak figuratively of the Word and God, as far as we are able. We must understand that just as a person's word is begotten from the soul without seed and beyond comprehension, so the Word is begotten from the Father. And as fire is begotten from fire and light from light, so the Son and Word of God is begotten from the Father.

Question 15. And how does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father?

Answer. You should not ask about this either, for this too cannot be put into words. Yet learn something about this as well. Just as a person's breath proceeds from the soul, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. And as Eve was neither begotten nor unbegotten but something in between, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. For Adam was unbegotten, Seth was begotten, and Eve proceeded. Eve was neither begotten, as Seth was begotten, nor was she unbegotten, as Adam was; rather she came forth from Adam's side. Adam was unbegotten as a figure of the unbegotten Father; Seth was begotten as a figure of the begotten Son; and Eve proceeded from Adam's side as a figure of the all-holy Spirit. For the Holy Trinity was prefigured in our first parents. But Adam, Seth and Eve were bodies, and were separate from one another, whereas God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are neither bodies nor separate from one another. Only the figure of the Father's unbegottenness is seen in the unbegotten Adam, the figure of the Son's begetting in the begotten Seth, and the figure of the Holy Spirit's procession is seen in Eve, who proceeded. Understand this matter too in this way.

Question 16. Is God contained in one place, or not?

Answer. Apply your mind and understand that God is light that cannot be seen or contained; God is neither seen nor contained anywhere. And since he is not contained even by the universe, how is it possible for him to appear or

to be understood by anyone? Neither Moses, who saw God, nor the disciples of his Word on that mountain of the Transfiguration, nor anyone else was ever able to behold the Godhead unveiled. So it is clear that God is not contained in one place but is present everywhere. So much for theology; from here on we will begin to speak about the economy, that is, about the incarnation of the Son and Word of God.

Question 17. Look, I am asking you a question; answer me. You have taught us about the Holy Trinity, that God has three hypostases, and that he is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Now I ask you: who is this Christ? I want to learn about him.

Answer. You have certainly heard about the Holy Trinity, that one person is called Father, another Son, and the other person is called Holy Spirit. Know, then, that this Son and Word of God the Father put on human flesh and walked on the earth as a man. He was therefore named Christ because he was anointed, that is, he put on human flesh. And for this reason he is called God incarnate, and Christ, the Son and Word of God, and God, because he put on human form.

Question 18. And what reason or what need did God, that is, the Son and Word of God, have to become incarnate and walk on the earth as a man?

Answer. God had no need at all to become incarnate; it was humanity that needed healing. For when God had made heaven and earth and everything in them, he also fashioned man, placed him in the middle of paradise, and appointed him king over all created things, so that all might serve him, and that he might dwell in paradise as the image of God. The devil, knowing this and envying man's dignity, counselled man to disobey God, so that through disobedience he might drive him out of paradise and out of the dignity God had given him, and make the immortal one mortal. And man, having no experience of the evil one's wickedness, listened to the devil's counsel and disobeyed God, and from then on he received the death of sin. Likewise all the people descended from him, receiving sin as if from their ancestors, held fast to it, and sin grew strong against humankind. God sent prophets and teachers into the world to teach the world, that is, humankind, so that they might turn from sin; but the prophets could not set things right. That is why God said within himself: “I will go down, put on flesh, and take human form; I will teach the creature I fashioned, and it will turn from the devil's counsel, and every human being will be like God, not by nature but by adoption.” And God, having willed this by the good pleasure of the Father and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit,

…the Son and Word of God came down and entered the pure womb of a virgin woman, and, taking flesh from her, became man. Then he came forth from the woman again, leaving her a pure, sealed and undefiled virgin, just as she had been before. He walked in the world among people as a man, and it was then that he was called Christ, because he was anointed and put on human flesh. And this is Christ, the Son and Word of God, who bears flesh.

Question 12. How could a virgin give birth to flesh and still remain a virgin? This seems wonderful to us and quite extraordinary. Please teach us about this too.

Answer. Even if this seems wonderful to us, it is not the work of a man but of God. For where God wills it, the order of nature is overcome. And again: "God is wonderful, and wonderful are his works." But hear various and very clear illustrations concerning the Virgin who gave birth. Remember that Adam, while a virgin, brought forth Eve and remained a virgin afterward, just as he had been before. And just as Adam brought forth as a virgin and remained a virgin, so too Mary the Mother of God, being a virgin, bore Christ and remained a virgin afterward.

Hear also another mystery bearing on this. Picture a house that is closed in on every side but has a small window facing east, made of clear and very thin glass. When the sun rises, its rays pass through the glass and enter, lighting up the whole house. And when the sun moves on and its rays go out again, the glass is not broken but remains unharmed by the rays of the sun striking it as they come in and go out. Think of the ever-virgin Mary in the same way. She, the all-pure one, is like a house closed in on every side. The Son and Word of God came down like a divine ray from the Father, the Sun of righteousness, entered through the glass window of her ears, and lit up her all-holy house. Then he came out again, in the way he alone knows, without harming her virginity in the least. Rather, he kept her a pure virgin before giving birth, in giving birth, and after giving birth.

Besides these, hear yet another illustration, radiant with light and most wonderful, and similar to the others. The pearl forms in the Red Sea, and it forms in this way. The shores of the Red Sea are dry, with only a little water spread over them. Throughout that Red Sea are found certain shelled sea creatures called pinnae. These pinnae always lie with their shells gaping open, waiting for food to nourish them. Now while they lie gaping and waiting for their food, lightning often strikes there, and a flash of lightning comes down on the pinna, and finding the pinna's shells

open, it enters it. The pinna at once contracts and clamps itself shut, enclosing the lightning inside. The lightning, winding itself into the (7) [?] of the pinna's eyes, makes them shine brightly and turns them into pearls. When the pearls come out of the pinna, they fall onto the shore of that sea, and that is how those who search for them find them.

Think of the incarnation of the Word in the same way. The sea is the world, and the Virgin is the shell. The Virgin stood in the temple like a pinna, waiting for the heavenly bread, Christ God. He came down and entered into her like lightning, and, wrapping himself within the inmost parts of her virginity, he made radiant the all-holy flesh which he took on when he became flesh. And so the Word of God was born from her like a pure and precious pearl, without union with a man.

And just as the pearl is both heavenly and earthly—heavenly by reason of the lightning, earthly by reason of its union with the pinna's eyes—so Christ too is both heavenly and earthly: heavenly in his divinity, earthly in his humanity. And just as the pearl is formed without the union of male and female, from lightning and the pinna, so Christ too was born without the union of male and female, from the divinity and the flesh of the Virgin. And just as when a pearl is crushed, it is often the material of the pinna's eyes that is crushed and broken up, while the brightness of the lightning suffers nothing—the brightness of the lightning remains unaffected, and only the material of the pinna's eyes is crushed and suffers—so you must understand it in the case of Christ. For when our Savior himself was scourged and suffered on the cross at the hands of the unbelieving Jews, only the material of the flesh, that is, the humanity, suffered, while the divinity remained impassible. By saying this you silence the Theopaschites and teach the economy of the incarnation. In this way, beloved, your doubt is resolved by the grace of Christ.

…and alone conquer the devil who had conquered it. So once again the wise God, knowing in advance that humanity alone, without the divinity, could not conquer, hid the divinity in the flesh itself. In this way the devil, seeing the flesh and not knowing that the divinity was hidden within that very flesh, would come forward and wrestle with Christ, and so be conquered by the hidden divinity. And that is just what happened.

A fisherman who wants to catch a fish does not cast a bare hook into the sea. Instead he cunningly covers the hook with a worm on the outside, and so throws it into the sea clothed in the worm. The fish sees only the worm. It does not know that the worm has the hook inside it, but thinks the worm is all there is, without any hook; and so it is deceived and caught by the hook. Christ did the same. He wished to catch the venomous fish that lurks in the boundless waters of the abyss—or rather the great dragon, the devil. He did not present himself to the devil in his bare divinity. Instead, with cunning, he used as the worm his all-holy flesh, which he put on without any mingling from the ever-virgin Mary, that most holy earth, as the divine David says: "I am a worm and not a man." With it he covered the most sacred hook, his cross that saves the world, by being nailed to it, wishing through it to conceal his own divinity. Deceived and caught by it, this venomous, snake-biting fish, the great dragon, the devil, who had driven man out of paradise and brought death upon him, was conquered and destroyed. So the divinity corresponds to the hook, and the humanity to the worm. The devil, seeing the human nature on the outside and not perceiving the divinity hidden within it, was deceived. He went for the humanity and was caught by the incomparable and invincible hook of the divinity; and so the great dragon, the devil, was conquered. That is why the Son and Word of God did not come in his bare divinity to hunt the devil, but put on flesh and came in that way. And this is the reason the incarnation took place.

The devil himself, when he once wished to deceive man and drive him out of paradise, did not approach Eve in his bare devilishness. He put on the serpent like flesh, approached her in that way, and deceived her. For the crafty one knew that if he approached her in his bare devilishness, he would not be able to deceive her. That is why he clothed himself with the serpent as with flesh, and deceived Eve through the flesh-bearing serpent. The serpent was visible, but the devil was not; and through the visible serpent the unseen serpent, the devil, was at work. For in the case of our first parents it was two natures in one person that brought about the fall. And just as then two natures, devilishness and serpenthood, were united in one person—the one nature, serpenthood, being visible, and the other, devilishness, invisible—and drove man out of paradise, so

in Christ two natures, divinity and humanity, were united in one person. The humanity was visible, but the divinity was not, and the unseen divinity was at work through the visible humanity. And these two good natures—divinity, I mean, and humanity—have now brought back into paradise the man who long ago was driven out of it. And this is the reason why God became flesh and became man. For to him belongs glory to endless ages. Amen.
